blocks.text: Before getting into operations and patterns, let's understand what a stack actually is and why it exists.
The Real World Analogy
Think about a pile of plates in a cafeteria.
You always place a new plate on top. You always pick a plate from the top. Nobody pulls a plate from the middle or the bottom.
That is exactly how a stack works.

A stack is a linear data structure that follows one simple rule: LIFO (Last In, First Out). This means the element added last is the first one to be removed, just like a stack of plates where you take the top plate first.
Step 1: push(10) → stack becomes [10]
Step 2: push(20) → stack becomes [10, 20]
Step 3: push(30) → stack becomes [10, 20, 30]
Step 4: pop() → removes 30 (last added)
Step 5: pop() → removes 20
Step 6: pop() → removes 10
A stack has two ends conceptually, but operations happen only at one end called the top. Elements are inserted (push) and removed (pop) only from the top, while the bottom remains unchanged.
Two ends  but only one end is ever used:

items: The top is the only place where elements are added (push) and removed (pop), so all operations happen at the same end.
The bottom element never moves or gets accessed directly, it just stays in place while changes happen only at the top.

Stack

The last element added is the first one removed
Operations happen at one end (top)

blocks.text: Think of a stack like a pile of books.
You can only touch the top book.

items: If you add a book (push), it goes on top → TOP moves up.
If you remove a book (pop), you take the top one → TOP moves down.

blocks.text:
You never touch the middle or bottom.
Only the top matters, that’s why stack needs just one pointer.

content.title: 4. How the Stack Works

items: When a new element is added, it is placed above the current top, and the top pointer moves up.
When an element is removed, it is taken from the top, and the top pointer moves down.
No operation is performed in the middle or at the bottom.

blocks.text: 1. Push (Insertion)

items: Adds a new element to the top of the stack.
After insertion, the top pointer is updated to this new element.
If the stack is full (in array implementation), it leads to overflow.

blocks.text: Key idea: Insert at top only.
2. Pop (Deletion)

items: Removes the element currently at the top.
After removal, the top pointer shifts to the next element below.
If the stack is empty, it leads to underflow.

blocks.text: Key idea: Remove from top only.
3. Peek (or Top)

items: Returns the value of the top element.
Does not remove it.
Useful when you just want to inspect the current top.

blocks.text: Key idea: Read top without modifying stack.
4. isEmpty

items: Checks whether the stack contains any elements.
Returns true if top is null (or -1 in arrays), otherwise false.

blocks.text: Key idea: Detect empty condition.
A stack can be implemented in two ways: using an array and using a linked list.
1. Stack Implementation Using Array
An array-based stack has a fixed size, meaning you must define its capacity before using it. Once the stack reaches this limit, no more elements can be added, which leads to overflow.
2. Stack Implementation Using Linked List
A linked list based stack does not have a fixed size. It grows and shrinks dynamically as elements are added or removed.
In this implementation, the top of the stack is represented by the head of the linked list, and there is no overflow unless the system runs out of memory.

Stacks are used in many real-world systems and problems you interact with daily. In a browser, when you visit pages, each page is pushed onto a stack, and pressing the back button pops the most recent page.
In text editors, every action you perform is pushed, and using undo simply pops the last action.
In programming, function calls are managed using a call stack, where each function call is pushed and removed when the function returns (pop).
Stacks are also used in expression evaluation, where compilers handle brackets and operators using stack operations.
In algorithms like Depth First Search (DFS), backtracking is handled using a stack, either explicitly or through recursion, where the call stack keeps track of the path.
